subject: Fysik
title: Forces and motion
sourceSummary: What a force is, that it is measured in newtons, and how gravity gives an object its weight — which is not the same thing as its mass. You also practise friction, how forces can cancel each other out, and calculating speed as distance divided by time.

questions.prompt: What unit is force measured in?
questions.opener: The unit is named after a famous physicist and abbreviated with a capital letter.
questions.explanation: Force is measured in newtons (N), and you can measure it with a dynamometer, a force meter with a spring. Kilogram is the unit for mass and tells you how much matter an object is made of, not how large a force is acting on it.

questions.prompt: You travel to the moon. What happens to your mass and your weight?
questions.opener: Mass is about how much matter you're made of, weight is about how hard you're pulled downward.
choices: Both your mass and your weight become smaller
Your mass stays the same but your weight becomes smaller
Your mass becomes smaller but your weight stays the same
Both your mass and your weight stay the same
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter in your body, and it stays the same wherever you travel. Weight, on the other hand, is the force of gravity acting on you, and since the moon is much smaller than the Earth it pulls more weakly — on the moon you weigh only about a sixth of what you do on Earth.

questions.prompt: On Earth, gravity is about 10 N per kilogram. What is the weight of a bag with a mass of 3 kg?
questions.opener: Multiply the mass in kilograms by 10 N/kg.
questions.explanation: Weight = mass · gravity per kilo = 3 kg · 10 N/kg = 30 N. Answering 3 N mixes up mass with weight — the number 3 is the mass in kilograms, not the force in newtons.

questions.prompt: Why is it harder to brake a bicycle on an icy road than on dry tarmac?
questions.opener: Braking relies on the force between the wheels and the road.
choices: The friction between the wheels and the ice is much smaller
The bicycle gains more mass on the ice
Friction becomes greater on ice and pushes the bicycle forwards
questions.explanation: Friction is the braking force between two surfaces moving against each other, and it is small between rubber and smooth ice. On dry tarmac the surfaces are much rougher, so friction becomes greater and the bicycle can therefore stop over a shorter distance.

questions.prompt: A box stands completely still on a table. What is true of the forces acting on the box?
questions.opener: Something must balance gravity, otherwise the box would fall.
choices: No forces at all act on the box
Only gravity acts, but it is too weak
Gravity pulling down and the table's force pushing up are equally large and cancel out
The table's upward force is greater than gravity
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls the box downward while the tabletop pushes back just as hard upward. The forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so they cancel out and the box stays still. If the table's force were greater, the box would instead lift off the table.

questions.prompt: A cyclist rides 30 km in 2 hours. What is the average speed?
questions.opener: Speed is distance divided by time.
questions.explanation: Speed = distance / time = 30 km / 2 h = 15 km/h. Answering 60 km/h means multiplying instead of dividing, which gives an unreasonably high speed for a bicycle.

questions.prompt: Emma runs 100 metres in 20 seconds. Calculate her average speed in metres per second.
questions.opener: The distance is already in metres and the time in seconds, so you can plug the values straight in.
steps: Write out the relationship: speed = distance / time.
Plug in the values: 100 m / 20 s.
The answer is 5 m/s, meaning 5 metres every second.
Sanity check: a walking person manages about 1.5 m/s, so 5 m/s is a good running speed.

questions.opener: Start with what a force is and finish with the speed formula.
questions.answer: Force: something that pulls or pushes and can change an object's speed, direction or shape · Unit: newton (N), measured with a dynamometer · Forces have both size and direction and are drawn as arrows · Gravity: the force that pulls everything towards the Earth's centre, about 10 N per kilogram · Weight = mass · 10 N/kg, for example 2 kg gives 20 N · Mass: the amount of matter, measured in kg, the same everywhere · Weight: a force, measured in N, smaller on the moon than on Earth · Friction: braking force between surfaces moving against each other, large against tarmac and sandpaper, small against ice and oil · Forces that are equal in size and opposite in direction cancel out, then the object stands still or moves at a steady speed · Speed = distance / time, unit m/s or km/h · 100 m in 20 s gives 5 m/s

questions.prompt: What do you use to measure a force?
questions.opener: The instrument often has a spring that stretches more the harder you pull.
questions.explanation: A dynamometer, a spring scale, measures force in newtons by stretching its spring different amounts depending on how hard you pull. A thermometer measures temperature and a stopwatch measures time.

questions.prompt: Gravity on Earth is about 10 N per kilogram. How large is the weight of a backpack with a mass of 5 kg?
questions.opener: Multiply the mass in kilograms by 10 N/kg.
questions.explanation: Weight = mass · gravity per kilo = 5 kg · 10 N/kg = 50 N. Answering 5 N confuses the mass with the weight.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between mass and weight?
questions.opener: One of these quantities changes when you travel to another celestial body, the other doesn't.
choices: They are exactly the same thing
Mass is measured in newtons, weight in kilograms
Mass is the amount of matter and stays constant, weight is a force that depends on where you are
Weight is constant everywhere in the universe
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and doesn't change no matter where it is, while weight is the force of gravity on the object and varies depending on the celestial body — for example, weight is smaller on the moon than on Earth. Mass is measured in kg, weight in newtons, not the other way around.

questions.prompt: Why is it easier to slip on smooth ice than on gravel?
questions.opener: Think about how much the surfaces "grip" each other in the two cases.
choices: The friction between the shoes and the ice is much smaller
The friction becomes greater on ice
questions.explanation: Ice is much smoother than gravel, so the friction between the shoes and the surface is much smaller, which makes it easier to slip. Gravity and mass aren't affected by which surface you're standing on.

questions.prompt: Two people each pull on one end of a rope with exactly the same force in opposite directions. What happens?
questions.opener: Think about what applies when two equally sized forces act in opposite directions.
choices: The rope accelerates in one direction
The forces cancel out and the rope stays still
questions.explanation: When two forces are equal in size but opposite in direction, they cancel out, so the total force on the rope is zero and it stays still. If one person pulled harder, the rope would instead move in that direction.

questions.prompt: A car drives 180 km in 3 hours. Calculate the car's average speed in km/h.
questions.opener: The distance is already in kilometres and the time in hours, so you can substitute directly.
steps: Write down the relationship: speed = distance / time.
Sanity check: 60 km/h is a common speed on a country road, so the answer matches reality.

questions.prompt: A cyclist keeps a speed of 20 km/h for 1.5 hours. How far has the cyclist travelled?
questions.opener: Rearrange the speed formula: distance = speed · time.
questions.explanation: Distance = speed · time = 20 km/h · 1.5 h = 30 km. Answering 13.3 km means dividing instead of multiplying.
